title: A broken DNSSEC rollover took down .al. Now 1.1.1.1 tells you when validation is bypassed
summary: When a failed DNSSEC key rollover took down the .AL TLD, we deployed a Negative Trust Anchor to restore resolution. This time, though, clients didn't have to take our word for it: 1.1.1.1 returned EDE 33, a new DNS error code that signals directly in the response that DNSSEC validation was bypassed.
body_text: On July 3, 2026, the Albanian communications authority (AKEP), the operator of the .al country-code top-level domain (TLD) of Albania, attempted a DNSSEC key rollover. Something went wrong, resulting in DNSSEC validation failures. Any validating DNS resolver receiving these signatures was required by the DNSSEC specification to reject them and return errors to clients. That includes 1.1.1.1 , the public DNS resolver operated by Cloudflare. The .al TLD is the online home of Albanian government services, banks, and media; it ranks #191 on Cloudflare Radar's TLD ranking . Anyone trying to visit those sites, using a validating resolver, found them unreachable during the incident. The failure had the potential to affect every .al domain, regardless of where it was hosted or which authoritative nameservers served it. Just two months earlier, a similar incident struck .de , the TLD of Germany. As we described in our blog post on the incident , our response was to install a Negative Trust Anchor (NTA) for .de , temporarily suspending DNSSEC validation in 1.1.1.1 to keep domains reachable while the registry resolved the issue. We did the same for . al . NTAs restore resolution, but silently. A client receiving a response served under an NTA has no way to tell, from the response alone, that DNSSEC validation was bypassed, leaving it unable to distinguish a legitimate answer from a spoofed one. For the .al incident, 1.1.1.1 addressed that gap for the first time, returning a new Extended DNS Error (EDE) code alongside every affected response to signal that the answer was not DNSSEC-validated due to the presence of an NTA. The graph below shows the SERVFAIL and NOERROR rates for .al queries on 1.1.1.1 throughout July 3. The SERVFAIL rate climbs as cached records expire and resolvers are forced to revalidate. It drops sharply when the NTA is applied at 17:15 UTC, restoring resolution. What happened to .al We discussed how DNSSEC works in more detail in our prior blog post . A brief recap: DNSSEC builds a chain of trust from the root zone down to individual domain names. The root zone holds a Delegation Signer (DS) record for each signed TLD, a fingerprint of that TLD's DNSKEY. A resolver verifying .al checks that the DNSKEY served by .al 's nameservers matches the DS record in the root. If it does, the resolver trusts that DNS responses from .al 's nameservers are authentic. The same pattern repeats one level down: .al holds DS records for its signed child zones, each with a matching DNSKEY. A break anywhere in that chain, such as a DS record pointing to a key that no longer exists, causes validation to fail for everything below it. Before the incident, the root zone held a DS record matching the DNSKEY served by the .al nameservers, as illustrated below. At around 14:15 UTC, the .al operator published a new DNSKEY and stopped serving the old one. The DS record in the root zone still pointed to the old DNSKEY (id=26319), so any resolver attempting to validate .al responses found no matching key and failed. At roughly 17:00 UTC, the .al operator removed the new DNSKEY without restoring the old one. The zone now had no DNSKEY records at all, while the DS record in the root still pointed to id=26319, and resolution continued to fail. At roughly 19:15 UTC, the .al operator removed the DS record from the root zone. Without a DS record, resolvers no longer expected DNSSEC validation for .al , and resolution was restored, though the entire TLD was now unsigned. As of publishing, .al remains unsigned. The DS record has not been restored to the root zone by the .al operators. Without a DS record, every .al domain is unable to use DNSSEC protections. Why Negative Trust Anchors are used Having a broken DNSSEC configuration can be painful, especially when it impacts an entire TLD at once. As we covered in our .de incident blog , recursive DNS operators can install a Negative Trust Anchor (NTA) as defined in RFC 7646 , which tells a resolver to treat a zone as unsigned and bypass validation. Before installing the NTA, we attempted to reach the .al operator directly and posted on the DNS-OARC Mattermost to alert the community. We received no response, in part because the operator's contact addresses were themselves under .al , making them unreachable during the outage. We applied the NTA for .al and rolled it out to all 1.1.1.1 users by 17:15 UTC, roughly three hours after the chain broke. The tradeoff is the same as it was for .de : a Negative Trust Anchor suspends DNSSEC validation, which means .al domains were no longer protected against DNS spoofing for the duration. We judged this acceptable for the same reason: the failure was public, confirmed, and affecting every validating resolver equally. The Negative Trust Anchor was removed the following day, once the .al operator had removed the DS record from the root zone. With no DS record present, resolvers no longer expected DNSSEC for .al and the NTA was no longer needed. The problem with Negative Trust Anchors Installing a Negative Trust Anchor is an aggressive measure. We suspend DNSSEC validation to keep domains reachable, accepting that responses are no longer cryptographically verified for the duration. Users get answers instead of SERVFAIL, but those answers carry no DNSSEC guarantee. What makes this harder is that, up until now, nothing in the DNS response signalled this to the client; a response served under an NTA looked identical to a fully validated one. RFC 7646 acknowledges this gap and recommends that operators publicly disclose which NTAs they have in place, but that disclosure is out-of-band. For both the .de and .al incidents we published status pages, but a status page requires the user to go looking. An application, a monitoring tool, or a user querying 1.1.1.1 had no way to tell, from the response alone, that DNSSEC validation was bypassed. Bringing transparency to Negative Trust Anchors Extended DNS Error (EDE) codes, defined in RFC 8914 , allow resolvers to include additional context alongside any DNS response, whether that is an error or a successful answer. Babak Farrokhi at Quad9 proposed an Internet-Draft to signal the presence of a Negative Trust Anchor directly in the DNS response, using a new EDE code: Disclosure of Negative Trust Anchors in DNS Responses . We joined as co-authors, and 1.1.1.1 now implements it. During the .al incident, any query for a .al name returned both the answer and the new EDE code while the Negative Trust Anchor was installed. Here is what that looked like: $ kdig @1.1.1.1 google.al ;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY; status: NOERROR; id: 32848 ;; Flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1; ANSWER: 1; AUTHORITY: 0; ADDITIONAL: 1 ;; EDNS PSEUDOSECTION: ;; Version: 0; flags: ; UDP size: 1232 B; ext-rcode: NOERROR ;; EDE: 9 (DNSKEY Missing): 'no SEP matching the DS found for al.' ;; EDE: 33 (Negative Trust Anchor): 'a Negative Trust Anchor has been applied for this query (see RFC 7646)' ;; ANSWER SECTION: google.al. 300 IN A 142.251.142.196 The response is a NOERROR with a valid answer: google.al resolves, but two EDE codes accompany it. EDE 9 (DNSKEY Missing) surfaces the underlying DNSSEC failure: the chain of trust was broken and validation failed. EDE 33 (Negative Trust Anchor) signals that 1.1.1.1 applied a Negative Trust Anchor and served the response anyway. Together they give clients and operators full visibility into what happened: the answer is real, but it was not DNSSEC-validated. 1.1.1.1 returns EDE 33 on any response generated while an NTA is active, regardless of whether the query itself would have failed DNSSEC validation. A query for a domain that does not use DNSSEC at all will still carry EDE 33 if it falls under an active NTA. This is intentional: the NTA covers the entire zone, and transparency applies equally to every response served under it. This also resolves an issue we flagged in our .de blog, where 1.1.1.1 incorrectly returned EDE 22 (No Reachable Authority) instead of surfacing the underlying DNSSEC error. During the .al incident, 1.1.1.1 correctly returned EDE 9 (DNSKEY Missing) alongside EDE 33. The Internet-Draft is an individual submission and EDE 33 has been assigned by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) . Thanks to our co-author, Babak Farrokhi at Quad9, the kdig tool from the Knot project now recognizes EDE 33 by name , and a pull request for Unbound is under review. We hope other resolver implementations will follow. The Internet-Draft has been submitted to the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) DNSOP Working Group , and will be discussed in the DNSOP Working Group at the IETF meeting, taking place in Vienna from July 18 to July 24. Closing the gap TLD-level DNSSEC failures are rare, but when they happen they affect every domain underneath the affected TLD simultaneously, and every validating resolver equally. The .al incident, following closely behind .de , shows that Negative Trust Anchors are a necessary operational tool, but one that has, until now, been invisible to the users they affect. EDE 33 closes a gap that RFC 7646 left open. A response served under a Negative Trust Anchor now says so directly, giving operators, monitoring tools, and users the information they need to understand what the resolver did and why. The Internet-Draft is available at the IETF datatracker . If you have thoughts on it, the IETF DNSOP mailing list is the right place to share them. If you want to learn more about how DNSSEC works, visit our page How does DNSSEC work? And you can always follow real-time DNS trends and TLD data on Cloudflare Radar .

title: The UK Government publishes its latest research into the fast-growing UK Artificial Intelligence sector.
summary: The UK Government’s Department for Science, Innovation and Technology , has published its latest sector research highlighting the rapid growth of the UK’s Artificial Intelligence sector. As one of the UK’s Industrial Strategy “frontier sectors”, AI is driving innovation, attracting investment
body_text: The UK Government’s Department for Science, Innovation and Technology , has published its latest sector research highlighting the rapid growth of the UK’s Artificial Intelligence sector. As one of the UK’s Industrial Strategy “frontier sectors”, AI is driving innovation, attracting investment, creating jobs, and strengthening the economy. Our AI research capability played a key role in deep-reading the web and official sources to identify the AI developers and AI diversified companies across the UK, helping to showcase the strength and breadth of this thriving ecosystem. The capability also provided the key insights about the products and services offered by the AI companies. Glass.AI has provided the necessary evidence for this annual analysis of the UK’s AI sector since 2022, contributing to the UK Government estimates of the scale, scope and growth of firms developing AI products and services. You can find here more details about our Agentic AI approach to automating sector and place research for Governments. Like in previous studies, given that Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes do not yet include a specific ‘artificial intelligence’ classification, the analyses contained in this report were based on a business-focused taxonomy that can better reflect AI activity in the UK. The taxonomy used to describe AI activity in this study is illustrated below: Key insights Companies : From 2023 to 2024, the number of AI firms jumped by 58% to around 5,800. Employment : UK AI sector employment grew by 33% to around 86,000. Revenue : Revenue saw a massive increase of 68%, reaching around £23.9 billion. Gross Value Added (GVA) : The sector’s GVA more than doubled, increasing by 103% to £11.8 billion. Investment : Investment in dedicated AI companies rebounded to £2.9 billion, surpassing the previous 2022 record. Conclusion The UK’s artificial intelligence sector has grown substantially over the past year across all core economic metrics. This increase in AI companies since 2023, driven by SMEs and micro-businesses, reflects widespread recognition of AI-enabled business opportunities across diverse economic sectors. A potential next step in this research to fully understand the size of the sector would involve looking at the adoption of AI. You can read the full UK AI report here . At Glass.AI, we are supporting many governments to understand and monitor their key emerging sectors, including the EU Commission , the Australian Government and others. If you’re interested in tracking one of these ‘impossible’ sectors in the UK or globally, please contact us at info@glass.ai .

title: Benefits of an Automated Payroll System for Remote Workers
summary: Stop struggling with global payroll. Automate currency conversions, tax compliance, and remote payments with Ontop. Simplify your international operations today.
body_text: Managing a global workforce becomes complex when handling multiple currencies, tax systems, and compliance standards. Manual processes not only consume valuable time but also increase the risk of costly errors. Automated solutions streamline these challenges and ensure accurate, on-time payments for remote teams. Automation simplifies currency conversions, tax calculations, and compliance management, allowing businesses to focus on growth rather than paperwork. This approach is particularly valuable when expanding a distributed workforce. Ontop's payroll software provides the tools needed to manage global payroll efficiently while minimizing administrative burdens. Summary Late payments hit a large share of freelancers at least occasionally, with many experiencing delays or non-payment more than half the time. This isn't an edge case problem. It's a structural failure in how cross-border payments work, creating income uncertainty that undermines the stability remote work promises. Compliance challenges affect 68% of payroll professionals managing international payments, according to the Global Payroll Payments Report. When two-thirds of the people responsible for processing payments struggle with regulatory requirements, that complexity cascades directly to contractors, leading to classification disputes, tax penalties, and payment delays as companies sort out jurisdictional rules. Currency management creates friction at scale, with 73% of payroll professionals identifying multi-currency handling as a top challenge. Traditional banking infrastructure extracts 2-4% from every international transfer through exchange spreads and intermediary fees, while conversion timing uncertainty makes income forecasting nearly impossible for contractors paid across borders. Automation eliminates up to 90% of payroll errors by removing manual data entry and calculation mistakes, according to QuotaPath research. When the same logic applies consistently to every transaction, payment amounts stop fluctuating unexpectedly, tax withholdings are calculated correctly, and contractors receive predictable income rather than spending hours reconciling discrepancies each payment cycle. Payment processing time drops by 80% through automation, compressing cycles from days to hours and eliminating delays that create cash-flow problems for remote workers. That speed shift isn't just convenience. It's the difference between planning confidently around known payment dates and building financial buffer days into every commitment, given that transfers arrive unpredictably. Digital nomad populations reached 35 million globally in 2024, revealing infrastructure gaps as more workers earn across borders while managing international logistics that require upfront commitments. Predictable payment timing, stable currency access, and proper documentation become essential when visa applications, housing deposits, and travel bookings demand proof of reliable income that traditional informal payment arrangements can't provide. Payroll software addresses these challenges by automating payment scheduling, compliance tracking, and currency handling across 150+ countries, providing distributed teams with the infrastructure reliability needed to sustain cross-border work. The Real Cost of Getting Paid the Old Way Traditional payment systems weren't made for global work . They were created for local transactions between companies and employees in the same country, using the same money and following the same tax rules. When these systems must operate across borders, they break down in predictable, costly ways . Non-payment isn't unusual. Late invoice payments are a common experience for freelancers. More concerning still, many freelancers are paid late, or not at all, more than half the time. This isn’t just about payment delays; it reflects a structural reliability issue that undermines the whole idea of remote work. Using efficient payroll software can help streamline these processes. International transfers can take days, and sometimes even a week if extra banks are involved. You send an invoice on the 30th, but the money might not arrive until the 8th or 10th of the next month. Currency exchange often quietly takes 2-4% off what lands in your account. You agree to $3,000, but after conversion and fees, only $2,850 shows up. That missing $150 isn’t explained in an email. It just disappears into the gap between what was promised and what actually arrived. How does payment uncertainty affect mental accounting? Mental accounting plays an important role in managing money. People determine whether problems arise from fees, exchange-rate changes, or errors in the financial system. They send follow-up emails across time zones, and it has become routine to check the bank app twice a day, wondering whether today is the day the payment will go through. This cognitive load doesn't appear on any bill, but it drains focus, time, and peace of mind. The main problem is often a lack of visibility. Deductions aren't clearly listed, and tax withholding can vary depending on an individual's classification. Contracts may not clearly specify payment timelines or indicate which party bears currency risk. When issues come up, people have to seek answers, often from those who understand the payment rails no better than they do. Does remote work flexibility lead to financial uncertainty? Remote work promises flexibility. You can work from anywhere, set your own schedule, and build a life that fits your needs. But that flexibility disappears when your income isn’t steady. Financial uncertainty makes it harder to commit to rent in a new city, book travel, or even decide if you can afford to take a week off between projects. What challenges do companies face with manual payment processes? The same issue comes up when hiring and building teams. Companies that depend on manual payment methods face similar problems. Finance teams spend many hours matching invoices, obtaining approvals, and managing currency conversions across various banking platforms. As the team grows from five contractors to fifteen, and then to thirty, the administrative burden increases. This leads to more payment errors, which frustrate contractors and erode trust. How can payment software improve payment logistics? Platforms such as payroll software make cross-border payments easier by providing automatic tax calculations, tracking compliance, and enabling instant payments. This reduces payment times from days to hours and eliminates manual reconciliation tasks that can lead to errors and delays. Automation not only saves time but also restores predictability for both the company and the people it pays. What extra responsibilities do contractors face? You agreed to deliver great work, and you did, but now you're handling a second job: payment logistics . This aspect is rarely discussed when considering the freedom of remote work . It includes keeping spreadsheets to track who owes you money, setting calendar reminders to follow up on late invoices, and the nagging worry that grows when rent is due, and the transfer still hasn't gone through. Most people avoid discussing this because it seems unprofessional. Saying you're worried about getting paid can make it seem like you don't trust your clients or that you haven't fixed this issue yet. So, you stay quiet, send polite reminders, and deal with the stress on your own. What is the biggest issue with current payment systems? The truth is, payment friction isn't a sign of failure; instead, it's a design flaw in systems that were never built for how we work today. When payroll systems can't keep up with global teamwork, the workers end up paying the price in time , money , and emotional energy . What other factors complicate payments? Geography alone does not explain why payments become complicated. Several other factors also contribute to this complexity, and understanding how payroll software can streamline these processes is crucial. Related Reading Paying Overseas Contractors Global Payroll Trends International Payroll Compliance Global Payroll Best Practices How to Pay Overseas Employees Global Payroll Strategy Cross Border Transaction Payroll for Remote Workers Why Cross-Border Work Makes Payroll More Complicated Geography multiplies every point of failure. A contractor in one country working for a company in another is not just dealing with distance. They are also dealing with different legal systems, tax rules, banking systems, and regulatory expectations that were never set up to work together. What works smoothly within borders can change when money needs to cross them. Exchange rates fluctuate frequently, yet most payment systems lock in rates at random times. For example, you agree to $5,000 for a project. The client sends it on the 15th, but by the time it shows up in your account on the 22nd, the rate has changed. Sometimes this works out well for you, but often it doesn't. That $5,000 can shrink to $4,850 after conversion costs and bank fees . The loss isn’t explained; it simply comes in lower than expected. Forecasting income becomes guesswork. If you are paid in a foreign currency, you can't know the exact amount you'll receive until it arrives. Planning for rent, savings, or business costs requires guessing currency fluctuations that you can't control. This instability worsens when managing multiple clients across multiple currencies. One month you might see an increase of 3% , and the next, a drop of 5% , neither of which truly shows the real value of your work. Our payroll software makes it easy to manage these challenges and ensure you receive the amounts you're expecting. How do different countries classify workers? Countries classify workers in different ways. Some view individuals as self-employed , while others expect employers to withhold taxes. A few require both sides to report the same income independently. If a company misinterprets local tax rules or workers misunderstand their responsibilities, either side may incur penalties or unexpected costs. Research from the Global Payroll Payments Report found that 68% of payroll professionals cite compliance with local rules as a big challenge. This issue is more than just a small administrative hassle; it becomes a barrier to growing global teams without risk. When two-thirds of those responsible for payments struggle with compliance, the contractors they pay feel that uncertainty. Even though tax treaties are in place, they are complicated and applied inconsistently. You might qualify for reduced withholding rates under a bilateral agreement, but only if both sides file the correct forms on time. If you miss a deadline or misunderstand a provision of the agreement, you could end up paying double taxes until the issue is resolved, which often requires costly professional assistance. What challenges do international wire transfers present? International wire transfers pass through correspondent banks, each of which charges a fee and slows the process. A payment sent from New York to Nairobi might go through three or four intermediary institutions before it arrives. Each institution charges fees and adds a day or two to the process. What should be a quick transaction becomes a week-long waiting game, leaving you unsure where the funds are or when they will clear. In some countries, it's hard to get access to stable-currency accounts or international payment platforms. Depending on where you live, opening a USD or EUR account locally can be tough or even impossible. This makes you depend on local-currency accounts, which can expose you to inflation risk, or on third-party services that add additional fees and exchange spreads. The infrastructure gap isn't your fault, but you're the one who ultimately bears the cost. Why is worker classification a risk? Are you an employee or a contractor? The answer depends on the laws of the country you are in. In one place, they might look at your work hours and decide that you are really an employee. This can lead to payroll taxes and benefits that the company did not expect. On the other hand, in another location, they might see the same situation as independent contracting, which means the employer has no responsibilities. This confusing area creates risk for both parties; however, contractors typically have less leverage to negotiate clarity up front. Misclassification isn't always intentional. Companies that are growing globally often do not realize that definitions of contractors can be different by country. They often use the same contract template across all locations, believing it is legally acceptable. When a disagreement arises or a tax authority reviews the relationship, the contractor is left trying to prove their status and protect their income. How can automation help with classification compliance? Platforms such as payroll software automate classification compliance by applying country-specific labor laws to each contract. This process points out misclassification risks before they become legal issues. Teams see that automation not only reduces administrative work but also eliminates the guesswork that often leads to costly compliance failures . Additionally, it helps protect contractors from getting caught in regulatory disputes that they did not cause. What financial challenges do contractors face? Many contractors cannot access the same financial services as local employees. In some areas, getting international cards is hard. Also, savings accounts that protect against currency exchange rate losses are not available everywhere. Payment platforms popular in one country may not integrate with the banking systems in another, making it difficult for contractors to arrange separate services just to receive and manage their funds. This disorganization creates significant inefficiency. Contractors may need one account to get payments, another to change currency at better rates, and a third to spend or save the money. Each transfer between accounts costs both time and fees. Plus, every extra service means one more login to keep track of, another set of terms to understand, and another chance for problems when something doesn’t work. How does complexity impact income across borders? As income crosses more borders, it creates more dependencies. Each currency conversion, banking intermediary, compliance rule, and classification confusion can become a potential failure point . When everything works well, it seems manageable. However, if a single part fails, the entire system can come to a halt. This leaves one looking for answers across time zones while bills are due. According to the Global Payroll Payments Report , 73% of payroll professionals report that managing multiple currencies is a significant challenge. This problem extends beyond finance departments; it affects employees, who face delays in transfers, confusing deductions, and uncertainty about their income. These issues undermine the stability remote work is meant to provide. What is the role of infrastructure in cross-border payments? Cross-border freedom is possible, but it requires infrastructure capable of handling complexit y without breaking down. When payments depend on manual work across systems that don't integrate well, each transaction becomes a complex negotiation with many issues. The important question is not whether problems will arise, but whether your payment system is designed to handle them or to make them worse. Automation is critical; it goes beyond speed and convenience. What an Automated Payroll System Actually Means for You It means predictability replaces guesswork. Payments arrive on schedule, not when someone remembers to process them. Currency conversions are clear, with a clear understanding of what you're getting and why. Human error is eliminated because the system handles all calculations, classifications, and compliance tracking without requiring manual input at each step. In contrast, manual payroll requires someone to initiate the process. They must remember the payment date, collect the required information, approve the transaction, and execute the transfer. Each step can cause delays, with approvals stuck in inboxes and invoices lost in email threads. Transfers often wait behind other tasks, making timely payment even harder. How does automation impact payment processes? Automation removes that dependency. Payments trigger based on predefined schedules . The system knows when contractors should be paid, pulls the necessary data from contracts and timesheets, calculates amounts, including any deductions or adjustments, and initiates transfers without manual intervention. You stop wondering if today’s the day someone will remember to pay you; the structure ensures it happens. Exchange rate uncertainty disappears when the system standardizes how conversions happen . Instead of finding out the final amount only after money lands in your account, automated platforms lock in rates at consistent points in the process and show exactly what you’ll receive. Fees get itemized , and spreads get disclosed . You see the breakdown before the transfer is complete , not days later when you’re trying to understand why the number doesn’t match your invoice. That visibility matters for budgeting. You can plan around actual amounts , not estimates. If you’re managing expenses in one currency while earning in another, knowing the converted value upfront lets you make decisions with confidence rather than hoping the exchange rate moves in your favor. What are the risks of manual payroll processes? Mistakes in spreadsheets can build up quickly. For example, someone might switch a number, make an incorrect calculation on a deduction, or apply the wrong tax rate. These errors can disrupt payroll cycles and create payment issues that take time to resolve. According to the QuotaPath Blog , automation can reduce payroll errors by 90% by eliminating manual data entry and calculation errors in traditional systems. Automated systems use consistent logic for every transaction. Tax rates are sourced from updated databases, and deductions align exactly with contract terms. Payment amounts align with agreed rates, preventing rounding errors or missed adjustments. When calculations follow the same method every time, mistakes disappear. This means payments do not change unexpectedly from month to month, eliminating the need to question whether changes are real or errors that need to be resolved. How does classification affect my income? Proper classification is critical to protecting income from legal risks. Automated platforms can track which rules apply to work arrangements by location and flag potential misclassification risks before contracts are signed . They also keep documentation that meets regulatory requirements in different countries. This structure is especially important during audits, tax season, or policy changes that could retroactively affect employment status. How does automation assist with compliance? Platforms like payroll software automate compliance by applying country-specific labor laws to each contract. They handle tax calculations across 150+ countries and keep audit trails that protect both parties from classification disputes. Automation not only saves administrative time but also eliminates regulatory guesswork that can lead to costly legal exposure , protecting contractors from compliance failures they didn't cause. You don't need to become an expert in international tax treaties or employment law. The system handles the complex details in the background and updates automatically as regulations change. This ensures your payments meet current requirements without requiring you to monitor policy changes across multiple countries. What is the significance of consistent payment timing? Financial stability isn't just about how much you earn; it's also about knowing when money will come in and being able to trust that timing. When payments arrive on time, you can sign a lease in a new city without worrying if this month's payment will show up before it's due. You can plan travel, buy new equipment, or take breaks between projects without worrying about cash flow. According to QuotaPath Blog , 80% of payroll processing time can be saved through automation. This change reduces payment cycles from days to hours and eliminates delays that create income uncertainty for remote workers and contractors. How does reliability change my work experience? Reliability significantly changes how you relate to your work. You can stop wasting mental energy on tracking payment status, allowing you to focus entirely on delivering excellent work . The stress of worrying about getting paid on time goes away. You are no longer juggling two roles: the job you were hired to do and the unpaid administrative burden of following up on payments. Automation is more than just a way for companies to be efficient; it helps create financial stability . When payroll works smoothly and predictably in the background, you can shift your focus from handling payment logistics to building the career and life that remote work was meant to offer. The Core Benefits of an Automated Payroll System for Workers Automated payroll replaces income uncertainty with financial confidence . Workers get paid on time, gain access to better currency tools, and avoid the traps that create tax problems. This change is not just about how things work; it shows a shift from worrying about getting paid to building a stable remote career. Payment delays often happen with manual processes. For example, an invoice approval might be lost, or finance might wait until once a week to process transfers rather than when they are due. Also, banks may hold funds for verification, which can take 24 hours to 5 business days. These are common issues. Many freelancers experience late payments or no payment more than half the time. This shows a system in which unreliability is the norm rather than the exception. How do automated systems eliminate payment bottlenecks? Automated systems eliminate payment bottlenecks by taking away human decision points from the payment chain. Contracts include payment dates, which help the platform trigger transfers automatically. Approvals are processed according to predefined rules, rather than waiting in someone's inbox. This means users don't have to check their bank accounts, wondering if today's the day the funds finally arrive. What changes when you know when payments arrive? Knowing exactly when payments arrive can change how you manage your finances. You can plan rent transfers without extra days for safety. Booking flights is also simpler, since you can do so confidently, knowing the funds will be available. You can take on projects based on their value, not just because you need quick cash to fill gaps caused by someone else's late payment. As a result, financial planning moves from guesswork to a process that you can actually control. How do traditional banks affect payment amounts? Traditional banks view international payments as rare transactions rather than a regular source of income. They use retail exchange rates, which deduct 2-4% from each transfer. On top of that, they have received fees, intermediary fees, and conversion fees that add up without clear notice. As a result, if you send a $3,000 payment, you might receive only $2,820 after the banking system takes its share. This means you might not realize there’s a loss until the money arrives. What are the advantages of modern payroll platforms? Modern payroll platforms provide USD-denominated accounts that skip multiple conversions. You are paid in a stable currency and can keep it without converting it. This lets you spend or save using tools made for global work. According to international payment providers like Visa, traditional bank fees on international transfers can range from 4% to 15% when you factor in all charges and exchange rates. This isn't just a minor convenience difference; it means hundreds or thousands of dollars per year stay in your account rather than being lost to bank fees. How do multi-currency accounts protect against volatility? Access to multi-currency accounts protects against local currency volatility . For example, if a home currency declines by 20% over a year , keeping earnings in USD or EUR helps maintain purchasing power. Users are not guessing on exchange rates; they are keeping money in the way they earned it. This allows them to convert at their preferred rates, using platforms they control. What role does automation play in error reduction? Research by Professor Raymond Panko found that up to 88% of spreadsheets contain errors, many serious enough to affect results. When these spreadsheets manage money, errors can result in incorrect payment amounts, incorrect tax deductions, or missed transfers. Fixing these problems can take weeks of back-and-forth communication. Using automated calculations greatly reduces this risk. Tax rates are sourced from updated rules in databases rather than relying on someone’s memory of last year's rules. body_text: The appointment demonstrates the tech founder’s commitment to celebrating Africa’s innovation and heritage on the global stage. November 19th, 2024: Flutterwave, Africa’s leading payments technology company announces that its Founder and CEO, Olugbenga ‘GB’ Agboola, has been appointed to the advisory board of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African Art. This appointment reflects Flutterwave’s continued commitment to supporting and celebrating African excellence across various sectors on the continent and beyond. The National Museum of African Art, the only U.S. museum devoted to the art of Africa, selected Mr. Agboola as one of seven new board members during its 60th anniversary year. This appointment places the Flutterwave Founder and CEO alongside leaders in academia, healthcare, and finance who will help shape the museum’s future direction. “It is a privilege to work with each of these new board members,” said John K. Lapiana, the museum’s director. “Our museum will benefit immeasurably from their perspectives and insight, especially now during our 60th anniversary year.” As a technology leader who has consistently worked to showcase African innovation on the global stage, Mr. Agboola brings unique insights to the museum’s mission of promoting cross-cultural understanding. His appointment creates an exciting bridge between Africa’s digital transformation and its rich cultural heritage. “It is an honor to support the National Museum of African Art in its mission to bring Africa’s vibrant heritage to a global audience. Olugbenga “GB” Agboola, Founder and CEO of Flutterwave and member of Smithsonian’s National Museum of African Art Board commented. “This opportunity aligns with Flutterwave’s vision of building solutions and contributing to opportunities that showcase Africa’s talent, potential, and innovation. I look forward to collaborating with the museum to highlight the connection between Africa’s cultural history and its future in the digital age” Mr. Agboola added. The National Museum of African Art’s collection includes over 13,000 artworks spanning more than 1,000 years of African history. As a board member, the Flutterwave founder and CEO will contribute to the museum’s efforts to showcase Africa’s artistic achievements to a global audience. Mr. Agboola also represents Flutterwave, as an inaugural member of the Milken Institute’s Africa Leaders Business Council. He serves on the boards of several prestigious organizations, like the U.S.-Africa Business Center of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, and the Corporate Council on Africa. Flutterwave has been recognized in Africa and globally for its payment innovations and role as an ecosystem enabler. The company was named Fast Company’s Most Innovative Company for Europe, the Middle East, and Africa in 2024. Flutterwave remains committed to supporting initiatives that celebrate African excellence in all its forms from technology to art.

title: Animation vs Slides in AI Video: What the Style Setting Controls
summary: Understand what an animation-versus-slides AI video setting may change, what it may not, and how to test style behaviour before a large render.
body_text: Use TRACE to test the setting Before applying one style across a course, run a controlled comparison with the TRACE framework. T, Task Choose a short, representative teaching task. Good tests contain something the visual must do: show a sequence, compare two states, locate a control, or explain a relationship. A generic welcome message reveals little about format behaviour. Use the same approved source and learning outcome for both versions. R, Record the configuration Capture: product and interface used; date and plan; input text or source version; style setting and template; duration, aspect ratio, voice, and brand configuration; any seed, model, or version information the product exposes. Without a record, a later difference may be mistaken for a style effect when another setting changed. A, Analyse the storyboard Before final rendering, compare: number and purpose of scenes; information omitted or added; text density; diagram and screenshot handling; transitions between ideas; warnings and exceptions; consistency with brand and source. If the product has no storyboard preview, make the first test deliberately short and low risk. C, Check the rendered behaviour Watch once with sound, once muted, and once without looking at the screen. With sound, check alignment and pace. Muted, check whether captions and visuals convey the necessary structure. Audio-only, check whether critical information exists solely on screen. This is a diagnostic exercise, not by itself a full accessibility audit. W3C’s WCAG guidance says captions for prerecorded audio in synchronised media are a Level A requirement, subject to its media-alternative exception. At Level AA, important visual details not conveyed in the main soundtrack may require audio description. A style switch can change those obligations by moving meaning into or out of the visuals. E, Evaluate and lock Use a short rubric: Does every visual serve the learning outcome? Is change represented accurately? Can learners control or revisit the pace? Are terms, warnings, and numbers correct? Is essential information available accessibly? Can this format be maintained at catalogue scale? Choose a baseline, document exceptions, and lock the settings for a production wave. Re-test after significant product or model changes. Decision examples Software login procedure A slide-style treatment may work if the main requirement is to show three screenshots with clear highlights. Animation is useful only if it makes cursor movement, state change, or sequence easier to follow. If animation replaces real interface details with a generic illustration, it may reduce transfer. How a pump moves fluid Animation can represent movement, pressure changes, and sequence over time. A slide-style version can still work if it uses a carefully designed series of static diagrams that learners control. Research on multimedia learning does not support assuming that animation always beats static graphics; pace and cognitive processing matter. Policy update A restrained slide-style video may suit a comparison of “old rule / new rule / required action.” Character animation may add no explanatory value. Keep the authoritative policy available as searchable text. Customer-service conversation Animation can show turn-taking, tone, and consequences in a scenario. Slides can show a transcript and decision points. The choice depends on whether the outcome is recognising wording, interpreting social cues, or following a process. For strategic topic selection, use the companion guide on choosing a training video format. To see current products and workflows, compare AI video tools for training and education and AI explainer video makers . Troubleshooting an unexpected result “Animation” looks like moving slides Check whether the mode promises object or character animation or only a dynamic style. The source may also be too abstract to suggest meaningful motion. Add a concrete process, states, and visual relationships, without inventing unsupported details. “Slides” changed my original deck Determine whether the tool imports editable slide objects, extracts content, or uses the deck only as reference. Those are different workflows. Exporting a deck to images may preserve appearance but can reduce editability and accessibility. Both settings look almost identical Confirm the style selection was saved, then compare storyboards and configuration. The product may share templates across modes, the content may not call for motion, or another style prompt may dominate. Ask the provider if behaviour is undocumented. The animated version is harder to follow Reduce decorative movement, split complex sequences into meaningful phases, add pauses, and let learners control playback. Synchronise narration with the action it explains. The slide version feels too dense Remove nonessential copy, turn headings into visual signals, split overloaded scenes, and put detailed reference material beside the video rather than inside every frame. FAQ Does animation mode animate every object? Not necessarily. “Animation” has no standard product-wide definition. Check current documentation and a preview. Does slides mode preserve my PowerPoint exactly? Only if the tool explicitly supports faithful import for the elements you use. Many AI tools extract or reinterpret slide content. Can I change style after generating the video? Some products allow restyling; others require partial or full regeneration. Check whether edits affect credits, timing, voice, and approved scenes. Which mode produces better learning? Neither universally. Choose the representation that makes the relevant structure, change, decision, or procedure clearest with manageable cognitive demand. Should a course use only one style? Consistency helps, but learning needs can justify documented exceptions. Keep shared voice, terminology, brand, and accessibility rules even when formats differ. Treat style as a testable production control The animation-versus-slides setting is best understood through evidence from your actual workflow. Hold the content constant, record the configuration, compare storyboards and renders, and decide against an instructional and accessibility rubric. Want to test source material in an animation-led workflow? Try Knowlify’s animated video maker , then verify current style behaviour and plan terms before standardising it across a course. title: Autopilot Update: First Commercial Customers & Selective Mode Is Live | Blend
summary: Autopilot's first commercial customers are live. See how AI adoption in mortgage lending is taking shape across lender types.
body_text: Last week, Autopilot became commercially available after 16 weeks and more than 25,500 production loans. Yesterday, we announced that five lenders have expanded their partnerships with Blend to include Autopilot, with more lenders exploring it. The first wave is not one type of lender. It spans a national fintech lender, two credit unions, a community bank, and a top mortgage servicer. That range matters. An AI agent that holds up across fintech speed, credit union member service, community bank relationships, and servicer scale is a strong signal. Subscribe to Autopilot updates A few things stand out about this group: They tested before they bought: Every one of these lenders made the decision after Autopilot ran on real production loans, not after a demo. The preview period existed so lenders could judge the agent on its actual work, and that is exactly what happened. One of them is brand new to Blend: One credit union in the first wave is adopting Autopilot as part of its initial Blend implementation. Autopilot is not just an upgrade for existing customers. It is becoming a reason lenders choose Blend in the first place. They are betting on pre-underwriting as the leverage point: During the preview, loans using Autopilot in pre-underwriting moved faster and converted at higher rates than comparable loans following standard workflows. The first wave saw those numbers on their own loans and decided the earliest part of the process is where AI pays off first. Onity Mortgage: co-building with a trusted AI partner Onity Mortgage (formerly PHH Mortgage) was working with Autopilot before most of the industry had heard the name. Over the preview period, the team put it to work across its consumer lending operation and watched what it did with real conditions on real files. “Onity Mortgage has seen consistent impact across all condition types surfacing and clearing conditions faster, resulting in quicker response times.” Colin Friday Senior Vice President of Consumer Lending, Onity Mortgage That is the pre-underwriting story. What comes next is more interesting: Onity is expanding its work with Blend beyond Autopilot itself, using the Blend MCP Server to build new AI-powered customer service experiences on top of verified loan data. “Onity Mortgage plans to use the MCP Server to power voice agents that can answer routine application-related questions with immediate, purposeful information, 24/7. For customers who prefer to speak with a person, it is about putting the right information in front of our teams the moment they need it. When a customer calls, our people should not have to search across multiple systems for an answer. The AI assistant can surface it for our support staff in real time so they can focus on the conversation and the customer experience.” Colin Friday Senior Vice President of Consumer Lending, Onity Mortgage This is the pattern we hoped to see when we opened the platform. Autopilot does the pre-underwriting work. The MCP Server turns the data it produces into a foundation lenders can build on, for their borrowers and for their own teams. Why the first wave signed on to Autopilot Mortgage origination has a timing problem. More than half of borrower activity happens outside 9-to-5 business hours, which means borrowers routinely go a day or more without a response from a loan officer. Autopilot closes that gap. It reviews documents as they are uploaded, compares them against lending guidelines, identifies missing or inconsistent information, infers GSE-driven qualifying income, and generates contextual follow-up requests while borrowers are still engaged. Issues get resolved during the application, not discovered days later. The lenders in the first wave did not sign because agentic AI is having a moment. They signed because they watched Autopilot clear conditions on their own loan files for four months and decided they did not want to go back. Selective Follow-up Mode is now live Two weeks ago, we gave you a first look at Selective , the follow-up mode lenders asked for during the trial. This week, it graduates from active development: Selective Follow-up Mode is now available in beta and production environments. A quick refresher on why it exists. Autopilot follows guidelines, which means it sometimes surfaces discrepancies that are technically accurate but too minor or subjective to justify contacting the borrower. Lenders wanted clear, high-confidence requests to go straight to borrowers while judgment calls got a human look first. Selective does exactly that. It evaluates each potential follow-up and routes it one of two ways: high-confidence requests go directly to the borrower, and lower-confidence ones surface in the loan officer feed as suggestions awaiting approval. Loan officers still see every proposed follow-up, so nothing is lost. The agent does the sorting. The loan officer stays in command. Selective will also become Autopilot’s default follow-up mode. That reflects how much confidence we have in this balance of automation and judgment, and how consistently lenders told us it is the right one. Lenders who prefer a different configuration can adjust it, but out of the box, Autopilot will now pair speed with a human checkpoint where it counts. This is also the fastest example yet of the loop we described last week. Lenders surfaced the problem during the trial, we built the fix alongside them, and it is now live for everyone. Contact your account team if you want help tuning Selective for your workflows. What comes next for Autopilot Commercial customers change what we ship, not how we ship it. Weekly updates continue, and the roadmap stays organized around the same three priorities: making the agent more dependable, giving lenders greater control, and opening the platform to new AI-powered workflows. On that last front, upcoming capabilities like Lender Chat will give lenders more ways to build on the same infrastructure Onity is using, whether they want to assist loan officers, automate internal processes, or create new borrower experiences. The first wave will not be the last. If the preview period taught us anything, it is that the best version of Autopilot gets built alongside the lenders using it.
